candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — dialysis vascular-access asepsis
candidate.educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and standardized vascular-access practices whenever an AV fistula is cannulated for hemodialysis.

options.A: Use clean technique for fistula cannulation because bloodstream-infection prevention measures are needed only when a dialysis catheter is accessed.
options.B: Skip access-site preparation when the fistula skin appears intact because visible cleanliness is sufficient after hand hygiene.
options.C: Reuse a vascular-access needle for the same client if it remains visibly clean because repeated cannulation does not require a new sterile device each time.
options.D: Use aseptic technique for vascular-access cannulation and follow standardized access-care practices each time the fistula is used.

candidate.rationale: CDC dialysis-safety resources emphasize staff education and competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique, and CDC provides specific AV fistula/graft cannulation checklists. More broadly, CDC intravascular-access guidance requires aseptic technique for insertion and care. D correctly adds aseptic access care to hand hygiene. A incorrectly limits infection-prevention measures to catheters, B omits access-site preparation based on appearance alone, and C proposes unsafe reuse of an access needle.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Dialysis infection prevention requires trained, competent vascular-access care using aseptic technique; CDC maintains standardized AV fistula/graft cannulation tools and requires aseptic technique for vascular-access care.
candidate.source_document_title: Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in Dialysis Setting; Dialysis Safety Resources & Tools

candidate.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention principle is essential?
